data.title: Spinal pole integrity and regulation during meiosis and mitosis.
data.description: Accurate partitioning of replicated chromosomes into daughter cells is fundamental for cell reproduction. Failure of this process during mitosis or meiosis could result in genetic disorders such as Down's syndrome. Moreover, normal development requires correct orientation and positioning of cell division plate which are determined by mitotic apparatus. In comparison to mechanisms of triggering mitosis, scant information is available about the mechanisms of mitotic progression. This research proposal aims at understanding mitotic progression as a network of gene activities reflecting protein interactions. Protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation play major roles in the regulation of mitotic progression. I propose to use mutants of fission yeast (S. pombe) plo1 kinase and a regulatory subunit of Drosophila protein phosphatise 2A, which both regulate mitotic progression, as genetical probes to dissect regulatory pathways. To identify plo1 interacting genes in fission yeast, we have isolated a number of mutants whose survival is dependent on modestsly high expression of plo1. Because growth of these mutants are sensitive to increased plo1 kinase activity, they are useful tools to identify plo1 interacting genes as suppressors. Both multicopy and chromosomal suppressors of the mutations will be analysed at molecular level. As plo1 kinase may be regulated through phosphorylation and the effects of the kinase will be reversed by some phosphatises, the genetical and biochemical interactions of a number of protein phosphatises with plo1 kinase will be tested. The 55kDa(B) subunit of Drosophila protein phospatase 2A is involved in spindle formation, chromatid separation and movement. I will examine the genetical and biochemical interactions of this enzyme with existing and newly identified genes also involved in these mitotic events. In addition I will test for possible involvement in a spindle assembly checkpoint, as a mutant of the budding yeast homologue shows the defects in the checkpoint. By using two genetic model organisms I hope to take full advantage of each genetic model system, and compare the regulatory mechanisms in the two organisms to understand the conservation and diversity of mitosis.

data.title: The 5-HT3 receptor: a model to define the structural determinants of function in ligand-gated ion channels.
data.description: Our understanding of the way in which ligand-gated ion channels work has been revolutionised by 9Å resolution images showing details of the secondary structure of the nicotinic acetylcholine (nACh) receptor from Torpedo electroplax. Comparison of images in the presence and absence of agonist has shown local structural changes both at the proposed agonist-binding site and in the a helices that are believed to line the ion channel. Yet, without the X-ray crystal structure of the protein, which has so far proved impossible to obtain, studies to identify those parts of the amino acid sequence forming the regions identified by electron microscopy have reached a barrier. I intend to address this problem using a homologous, yet homo-oligomeric, protein, the 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT)3 receptor subunit, using site-directed mutagenesis to insert putative N-glycosylation sites in the primary amino acid sequence. Only those located extracellularly will be glycosylated. I then intend to examine conformational changes that occur in a helices in two regions, the ligand-binding site and the ion pore, and thereby link the amino acid sequence and structural data. I will do this by insertion of histidine residues to create metal ion-binding sites. If two or more histidine residues are in a suitable orientation and proximity then they will create a binding site for metal ions, and, in the presence of such ions, relative movement between a helices will be blocked. The advantage of this method is that the functional integrity of the mutant protein can be monitored before and after adding metal ions. This technique has not been used before for the study of ligand-gated ion channels, but has been successful in identifying movement between a-helices in other families of neurotransmitter receptors. On a more speculative note, I also intend to use the over expression system we have developed to produce large amounts of pure receptor to explore the possibility of obtaining protein crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction studies.

data.title: The control of cell surface MHC class I expression by cellular and viral gene products.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Patrick Sissons, Prof John Trowsdale
data.description: Regulation of the Transporter Associated with Antigen Processing (TAP) by Endogenous and Viral Gene Products The MHC class I presentation pathway allows intracellular peptides to be displayed at the cell surface to cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL), and is of fundamental importance in defence against intracellular pathogens. The presentation of peptide to CTL is the final step in a complex intracellular process which involves the cytosolic degradation of protein to peptide, the transport of peptide to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP), and the loading and subsequent transport of class I molecules. TAP forms part of a complex intracellular structure, whose correct assembly is essential for efficient MHC class I presentation. The minimal components of this complex include TAP 1 and 2, class I heavy chain, ß2M, calreticulin and the newly identified tapasin protein. Tapasin plays a critical role in the presentation of antigenic peptides, it forms a bridge between TAP and class I and in its absence, cell surface class I is reduced, as seen in the mutant .220 cell line. In tapasin deficient cells, TAP mediated peptide translocation is reduced, a defect which is corrected following tapasin transfection. These results suggest that tapasin may regulate peptide translocation across TAP. Conversely, I have identified the HCMV encoded US6 glycoprotein as a viral inhibitor of peptide translocation. US6 binds to the TAP complex and inhibits peptide translocation, thus preventing loading and transport of MHC class I molecules to the cell surface. In this project the mechanism of action of the positive (tapasin) and negative (US6) regulator of TAP will be addressed. I will make tapasin mutants to determine the site(s) of interaction with TAP and class I. The effect of tapasin on peptide binding to TAP and ATP hydrolysis will be examined. US6 mutants will be generated to determine if US6 binds directly or indirectly to TAP, and which portion of the molecule is responsible for TAP inhibition. I will make a US6 deletion virus to determine the functional effects of US6 on viral inhibition of MHC class I presentation. Other functions of TAP remain poorly understood, specifically the regulation of assembly of the TAP complex, and is likely to require interaction with other proteins. Tapasin antisera immunoprecipitates 4 previously unidentified proteins which may be involved in the regulation of assembly of the TAP complex. These proteins will be isolated and sequenced, and their role in MHC class I assembly determined.

data.title: Genetics susceptibility in systemic lupus erythematosus.
data.description: Human systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease of unknown aetiology. There is a genetic component to disease predisposition, but the nature of the underlying genes largely remains to be determined. The aim of this proposal is to identify disease susceptibility genes that predispose to SLE. There are a number of difficulties inherent in conducting a genome- wide scan for disease susceptibility to loci linked to human lupus. However, there are several murine strains that spontaneously develop a lupus-like illness that have been utilized to investigate the pathogenesis of SLE. This proposal comprises two related aspects of the investigation of the genetic basis of SLE. It is intended to generate mice that are congenic for intervals on chromosomes 1, 4 and 7. These genetic intervals have been mapped in the New Zealand hybrid mouse model of lupus to be linked with the development of lupus in several different genetic crosses. By successive backcrossing and genetic screening, these congenic mice will be used to narrow the interval in which aetiological alleles are contained. Smaller intervals will permit a more rational choice of candidate genes for analysis, and eventually enable direct positional cloning of disease susceptibility genes. As regards the genetic analysis of human SLE, it is proposed to perform linkage disequilibrium mapping in patients with lupus nephritis. Mapping will be performed selectively, using microsatellite markers, and known or novel genetic polymorphisms on regions of the human genome that are syntenic with the loci mapped on mouse chromosomes 1, 4 and 7. These are the loci mapped to be in most consistent linkage with murine lupus and loci that are the subject of the congenic studies outlined above. A linkage disequilibrium analysis necessitates the use of marker alleles within 1-2 centiMorgans of the disease allele. Hence a genome-wide screen using this methodology is logistically difficult. However, this approach is well-suited to the type of directed analysis proposed. Linkage disequilibrium methods have the advantage over allele-sharing methods (used to investigate linkage in other complex human diseases) that the former only require families with single affected individuals. Allele-sharing methods are dependent on multi-case families which have limited availability in human SLE. Linkage disequilibrium mapping can also be used to investigate the allelic associations with SLE, such as the association between an FC? receptor gene polymorphism and lupus nephritis. This FCy receptor gene is situated on human chromosome 1q21-q22, which is syntenic with the region on mouse chromosome 1 listed above.

data.title: A structural and functional analysis of predicted ligand binding and targeting domains of polycystin-1.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof John Paul Luzio, Prof Martin Bobrow
data.description: The aims of this study are to develop and utilise reagents and model systems for the investigation of the structure and function of polycystin, the protein product of the autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease gene 1 (PKD1) and its role in the pathogenesis of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The function of this large putative membrane glycoprotein is unknown. The disease phenotype suggests it has a role in epithelial cell differentiation possibly via cell-cell or cell-matrix interactions at domains predicted by weak homologies to known proteins. Polycystin-specific reagents and existing well characterised in vitro models of epithelial cell development and function will be used to investigate its normal cellular function. To determine (1) the normal function of plycystin (2) its functional domains (3) other molecules with which it interacts and (4) how specific mutations cause the disease phenotype, two main reagents have been generated. A unique 14 kb full length PKD1 gene expression construct will be used to derive mutated constructs to investigate functional domains and the glycosylation, phosphorylation, and membrane targeting signals of polycystin using in vitro expression and transfection experiments. A panel of anti-polycystin antibodies has been used to demonstrate expression in tissues and cell lines including the well characterised MDCK model of epithelial cell function and tubular morphogenesis. Polycystin expression in vitro is confined to the lateral membranes of adjacent proliferative cells and is temporally expressed during formation of desmosomes, tight junctions and apical membranes. Its function will be investigated in these systems using transfection and over expression, domain specific antibodies, recombinant proteins and anti-sense constructs and measures of tight junction formation, cell proliferation and polarisation, adhesion and aggregation assays and cyst and tubule formation in culture. Interacting proteins will be determined using co-immunoprecipitation and the yeast two-hybrid system. To investigate the function of polycystin in vivo and generate a specific animal model of ADPKD, a mouse PKD1 null mutation will be engineered. The mouse 129 strain PKD1 gene has been cloned and used to construct a replacement gene targeting vector for electroporation into mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells. A promotorless IRES-selectable marker (pGT1.8IRESßgeo SA-IRRES-lacZ-Neo-SV40polyA) cassette has been cloned in to intron 15 following deletion of exons 16 to 21 which is predicted to form a truncated transcript and protein. Studies will concentrate on the effects of heterozygous and homozygous mutations on renal development and the whole animal and cellular phenotype.

data.title: Coated vesicle adaptors.
data.description: Adaptors, or APs, are heterotetrameric protein complexes involved in vesicle budding. The AP-1 and AP-2 adaptors are associated with clathrin-coated pits and vesicles at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and plasma membrane respectively. We plan to investigate the mechanisms by which AP-1 and AP-2 are recruited onto the appropriate membrane, and how this leads to the production of a coated vesicle. We will identify adaptor-binding proteins which might act as membrane docking sites by cross-linking, affinity purification, and two- hybrid library screening, and we will clone and sequence their corresponding cDNAs. We also plan to clone cDNAs encoding some of the minor proteins of unknown function that co-purify with clathrin-coated vesicles. Characterisation of these proteins will include immunolocalisation studies at both the light and electron microscope levels, transfecting tissue culture cells with both wild-type and mutant constructs and then examining the phenotype, and adding antibodies and/or constructs to in vitro systems that we have developed to determine at what stage a particular protein acts. The second aim of the proposal is to identify and characterise novel adaptor- related complexes. We have recently discovered an adaptor-like complex, AP-3, which is not associated with clathrin, and we plan to establish its function by antibody microinjection, by expressing truncated subunits that might act as dominant mutants, and in particular by taking advantage of the finding that two of the subunits are encoded by genes for which mutations are already known. In addition, we have evidence for at least one other adaptor-related complex, and we plan to investigate both its subunit composition and its function.

data.title: Communication impairments in children: causes, correlates and outcomes.
data.description: Children with specific language impairment (SLI) fail to develop language at the normal rate, for no apparent cause. This programme is concerned with the causes of SLI, both in terms of underlying cognitive processes, and in terms of etiology. One theory maintains that a basic problem in auditory perception is at the root of SLI, with language difficulties as a secondary consequence. The ways in which auditory perceptual problems can affect language learning will be explored by assessing language development in children with mild hearing losses, and by modelling the effects of degraded auditory input on language learning in a computer simulation. Auditory discrimination will also be investigated directly in children with SLI, by recording electrical brain responses to different sounds; the effects of training auditory discrimination will also be examined. At the etiological level, twin studies reveal significant heritability for SLI, but results vary depending on how the phenotype is defined. This study will consider which aspects of SLI are most heritable, and will look for environmental correlates of non-heritable deficits. In addition, heterogeneity of SLI will be explored by studies aimed at pinpointing the nature of "pragmatic language impairment", which is diagnosed when a child who can produce complex language fails to use it appropriately.

data.title: The molecular basis of specificity in tyrosine kinase-mediated signal transduction: cellular distribution to structural-thermodynamic correlation.
data.description: Many biological processes are based on equilibrium interactions, and hence are regulated by the effects of localised concentrations of biomolecules and their physiological ligands. It is apparent that in a large number of these interactions the binding is relatively weak such that high concentrations of non-specific molecules could give rise to an inappropriate biological outcome. Many of the interactions associated with intracellular signal transduction involve the equilibrium binding of upstream and downstream effectors of a given protein in a signalling pathway. Aberrancies in these pathways are responsible for many disease states. Only by characterising these interactions in terms of how they maintain the mutual exclusivity of given pathways can we understand these biological processes and, furthermore suggest routes for pharmaceutical intervention. In the tyrosine kinase mediated pathways distinct, independent domains of a protein are often involved in these equilibrium interactions. This suggests that some high level of specificity has to be imposed by these domain interactions. In this proposal the issue of specificity in interactions involving protein domains involved in tyrosine kinase signalling is addressed. This is to be achieved determining the thermodynamic-structural relationship for interactions focusing on two key areas : 1) The effect of multiple domains in imposing specificity in protein interactions and the implications of this to parallel processing of intracellular signalling, and 2) The role of water in defining specificity in protein-ligand interactions. Will involve isothermal titration calorimetric (ITC) binding studies coupled with mutagenesis and phage display methods on two systems (the ;85 subunit of PI3-kinase and ZAP-70) which exhibit binding to ligands via two Src homology (SH)2 domains. Experiments will discern the changes in binding parameters observed for the interaction of the two SH2 domains (and the inter-SH2 domain structures) and compare these with the interactions of single SH2 domains. The thermodynamic effect of incorporating water into biomolecular interfaces is not well-characterised. This part of the proposal will involve the continuation of work on the identification of water molecules in biomolecular interfaces. A combination of ITC, electrospray ionisation mass spectral and NMR data will be used to assess the strength of interactions of individual water molecules in an interface. As well as assessing the role of water in binding between interacting biomolecules, it will provide invaluable information to aid in structure-based ligand design and refinement of high resolution biomolecular structures.

data.title: Structural studies of extracellular matrix proteins and their receptors in development and disease.
data.description: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is an intricate network composed of large glycol-proteins and proteoglycans. It conveys mechanical stability to higher organisms, but also plays a key role in morphogenic processes such as embryogenesis and would healing. Most ECM proteins are not amenable to crystallographic studies in their native form, but individual modules of tandems can be expressed as recombinant proteins for structural studies. The aim of the present collaborative project is the structure determination of several ECM protein fragments to gain an understanding of the biological functions of their parent molecules. We plan to determine the structure of a functionally relevant heparin complex of endostatin, a potently anti- angiogenic collagen XVIII fragment. We also want to study the enditre trimeric non-collageneous NC1 domain to see how it directs triple helix assembly and to understand the mechanism of proteolytic endosatin release. Fibulin-2 is a dimeric microfibrillar protein associated with fibronectin and fibrillin-1. We would like to solve the structure of the N-terminal disulphide-rich domain involved in dimerisation and that of a tandem of calcium-binding EGF-like modules involved in ligand binding. Mutations in cartilage oligomeric matrix protein cause pseudoachondroplasia and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. A structure determination of the tandem of type III repeats, which resemble the EF-hand motif for calcium binding, will reveal how mutations in calcium- binding residues cause disease. Laminin is a large heterotrimeric protein that forms a network in basement membranes. The calcium-dependent assembly is mediated by the N-terminal LN domains of all three chains and we plan to study this process by determining LN domain structures, both in isoloation and in complex with each other. We also want to study the laminin LG domains involved in integrin binding. Finally, we will continue our work on collagen binding to proteins of the osteonectin family and would like to determine the structures of C. elegans osteonectin and testican.

data.title: Cell polarity and cell fate determination in C. elegans.
data.description: During embryogenesis, patterning events are critical to direct the spatial organisation of the developing animal. I propose to investigate patterning mechanisms that operate in the C. elegans embryo. C. elegans is an excellent system for this work, because powerful genetics and molecular methods can be combined with cell biology to examine developmental controls at single cell resolution. Furthermore, the soon to be completed genomic sequence and rapid reverse genetic methodology are facilitating new avenues of research. I propose to investigate two embryonic patterning events: the early choice of cell division axis orientation, which leads to proper cell positioning and inheritance, and the patterning of posterior tissues later in embryogenesis. The orientation along which a cell divides can be crucial for its subsequent development, and how it is chosen is regulated in organisms ranging from yeast to vertebrates. In C. elegans, where the orientations of early cell division axes are completely reproducible, it is one of the first indications of pattern. In previous work, I showed that the gpb-1 gene, which encodes a beta subunit of heterotrimeric GTP-binding protein, is required for the correct spatial orientation of early embryonic cleavages. In its absence, cell division axes are randomised. This is the only gene known to specifically affect axis orientation, an provides a means for investigating how axes are chosen and what polarity cues are used for orientation. To understand this process better, I propose to study further gpb-1 and identify and characterise molecules with which it interacts. Subsequent patterning events direct the establishment of body plans and the organisation of tissues. I have been studying how the posterior end is patterned. I initially showed that the gene vab-7 encodes an even-skipped homologue required for patterning posterior mesodermal and ectodermal tissues in the embryo. Using this information as a starting point, I have worked out an outline pathway of posterior embryonic patterning. I propose to use genetic and molecular methods to identify and study new genes involved to extend the pathway further, and to investigate the interactions between genes more precisely. This should allow me to understand what patterning means at the molecular and cellular level. vab-7 has a sequence and expression pattern similar to those of even-skipped homologues in other animals, including vertebrates, therefore this work should be directly relevant to other systems.

data.title: Genetic mechanisms in congential heart disease.
data.description: Localised tissue hypoxia is a major factor in the pathogenesis of myocardial infarction and cerebral stroke. The transcription factor HIF-1, consisting of HIF-1a and HIF-1ß proteins, is essential for the transcriptional response to hypoxia. HIF-1 DNA-binding and transactivation activity is induced by hypoxia. This results from the stabilisation of the HIF-1a protein, and a marked increase in the transactivation potential of the HIF-1a C-terminus. HIF-1 recruits the transcriptional adaptors p300/CBP, and activates transcription of several hypoxia induced genes. The HIF-1a C-terminus directly binds p300/CBP. I have cloned a novel protein (p35) that is induced by hypoxia, also directly binds p300/CBP, blocks HIF-1a nomdomg tp p300 in vitro, and inhibits HIF-1a activated transcription. p35 may function as an inhibitor of HIF-1a transactivation during normoxia, and as an autoregulator of hypoxia activated transcription. Understanding the role of modulators such as p35 should provide important insights as to how the complexity of the physiological response to hypoxia is achieved. Moreover, p35 and p300/CBP could serve as targets for drugs that enhance the cellular response to hypoxia.

data.title: Molecular physiology of alpha-intercalated cells in health and disease.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Martin Bobrow, Prof Patrick Sissons
data.description: The kidney plays a central role in maintaining normal acid-base homeostasis, which is essential for a wide variety of metabolic functions. Derangements in renal hydrogen ion secretion or reclamation of bicarbonate have far-reaching consequence, including development of nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis and failure of preservation of bone integrity. However, the physiological pathways governing renal acid-base balance, and their effects on tubular calcium handling, remain poorly understood at the molecular level, and are unlikely to be determined by physiological analysis alone. The advent of powerful molecular tools now permits the elucidation of these physiological pathways by initial identification of genes involved in rare mendelian disorders imparting a large phenotypic effect. Primary distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) provides such a model. Both autosomal dominant and recessive kindreds are reported, the latter often in association with sensorineural deafness. Those affected developnephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis and rickets. Mutations in the C1-HCO3 exchanger gene AE1 are responsible for dominant disease in all kindreds reported to date; a de novo mutation occurs in one I have studied. However, genes involved in recessive disease have not been identified. I have recruited 20 hearing and 8 deaf recessive dRTA families, often consanguineous, together with some 40 'sporadic' cases. These kindreds represent a unique and unrivalled collection and importantly, provide not only a mass of new clinical and biochemical information about dRTA, but also the necessary statistical power for pursuing a general linkage approach. In preliminary studies, these families have enabled me to exclude AE1 as a candidate gene in recessive disease. Having performed a 20 cM genome-wide linkage screen, I have now identified the first of at least two loci for hearing disease. The lod score of 8.1, with a=0.4, indicates odds of 100 million to 1 in favour of linkage. Therefore the studies proposed here include: The identification and characterisation of rdRTA1, the first gene for recessive dRTA. This will involve further refinement of the linked region with additional markers, genetic database searches and physical mapping to identify candidates homologous t already-known genes, followed if necessary by cloning of novel genes in the region. Analysis of the prevalence and spectrum of mutations in rdRTA1 in patients with both recessive and sporadic disease. Anatomical characterisation of rdRTA1, including the tissue distribution of rdRTA1, and cellular localisation of both wild-type and mutant proteins within the kidney. Functional characterisation of rdRTA1. Comparative functional analyses of expressed wild-type and mutant proteins in polarised and non-polarised cell systems will be employed to provide lessons in the normal and altered physiological pathway of rdRTA1, and to assess the contribution of defects in this pathway to the development of calcium-deposition disease, an important clinical problem. Investigation of genotype-phenotype correlation, firstly to refine phenotypic diagnosis and secondly to address the question of improving therapy. Similar studies to identify further causative genes in hearing and deaf disease. These investigations will provide crucial links between structure and function, and permit elucidation of disease processes in RTA. This in turn will help clarify the normal physiology of acid-base balance and renal calcium handling. The studies illustrate the utility of developing molecular genetic approaches both for studying renal physiology and moving towards improving care in the long term.

data.title: Glasgow Biomedical Research Centre.
data.description: A new Centre for Biomedical Research, based in a well-resourced new building, is proposed. The prime function of the Centre will be to provide the crucial collaborative environment necessary to advance the understanding of molecular processes in disease and immunity and to link basic and clinical scientists in the quest for new therapeutic strategies. To achieve this, it is proposed that several of the University's leading research groups, ranging from structural biology through microbiology, parasitology and immunology to clinical medicine, are accommodated in a building designed specifically to enhance multidisciplinary research and the flow of ideas, on a solid technological platform. The groups are presently housed in 5 different buildings which are scattered across the campus and the city. By bringing these groups together from 3 faculties, many would be exposed to disciplines they would not encounter otherwise, creating the conditions for considerable added value, such as the development of novel medical treatments and the application of basic approaches to understanding disease transmission and control. There are a number of strong clinical research groups with a direct and growing interest in immunology who are located remotely from the basic immunologists. The proposed Centre not only would solve these problems, but also would create synergy amongst the various groups, giving added value and setting the scene for application of basic research to more applied areas.
data.Other Applicant(s): Prof Neil W Isaacs, Prof David Barry, Prof Andrew Tait, Prof John R Coggins

data.title: Patterns and process in human genetic diversity: from genomes to populations.
data.description: European populations with different histories will be examined at high resolution using multiple polymorphic Y markers. Comparisons with the broader context of European diversity and with mtDNA and autosomal data will allow the relationship between Y diversity and population structure, and the differential contributions of males and females to gene pools, to be explored in details. Novel markers, informative in specific populations, will be identified for this purpose. Mutation at multialelic loci will be investigated, both as a tool for dating the origins of lineages, and for the fundamental insights provided into haploid mutation processes. Comparison of Y haplotypes of males suffering from infertility, testicular cancer and prostate cancer with those of controls provides a novel way to investigate whether negative selection is acting on Y haplotypes through these deleterious phenotypes. These studies also have the potential to provide exciting new insights into the aetiology of infertility (which has undoubted Y involvement) by clarifying the role of the Y and its population variability, and these will be pursued.

data.title: Deciphering the mechanisms that process stalled and collapsed replication forks and meiotic DNA double strand breaks in eukaryotes.
data.description: The central aim of this research is to extend our knowledge of recombination and DNA repair in eukaryotes. There are three main objectives: to identify the first examples of proteins that branch migrate and resolve Holliday junctions in eukaryotic nuclear DNA; study how and why different proteins target X-junctions; and initiate studies of presynapsis by reconstituting double- strand break (DSB) formation in vitro. Objective 1 will involve screening protein extracts for activities associated with processing model recombination intermediates and a novel genetic screen that uses a nuclear targeted resolvase to complement recombination/repair mutants of Schzosaccharomyces pombe. The second objective will involve structure-function studies of Sp[cce1 and YM03 from Saccharomyces cerevisae that each contain a novel motif which appears to be required for structure-specific DNA binding. These studies should elucidate a novel strategy for targeting X-junctions. Objective 2 will also entail detailed biochemical and genetic analyses of aNAC and BTF3 from S. pombe that I have recently identified from biochemical screen for X-junction binding activities. This work should provide clues as to how aNAC and BTF3 function during transcription and possibly other processes such as recombination/repair. Finally, objective 3 will involve biochemical characterisation of Rec12 that is believed to be the catalytic component for DSB formation during meiosis in S. pombe. Rec12's ability to bind and cleave DNA in vitro will be analysed and interactions with other proteins will be sought. These studies should determine more precisely how meiotic recombination is initiated.

data.title: Interactions between proteins bound at distant sites on DNA molecules: Accessory proteins and sequences in Xer site-specific recombination.
data.description: The proposed work arises out of my studies of the DNA binding activities of the Escherichia coli aminopeptidase PepA. This multifunctional protein is involved in transcriptional regulation, the activation of Xere site-specific recombination, and degradation of polypeptides in E. coli, and has homologues in a wide variety of species. PepA binds to distant sites on DNA and forms highly organised, nucleosome-like protein-DNA complexes in which the two participating DNA sites are interwrapped. PepA binds to DNA co-operatively with at least two other E. coli transcriptional regulators, ArgR and ArcA, and DNA binding is enhanced by DNA supercoiling. PepA ensures that only intramolecular Xer recombination occurs at plasmid sites, thus increasing the stable inheritance of plasmids in bacterial cultures. The protein-DNA and protein-protein interactions and the DNA dynamics important for formation of PepA-DNA complexes will be investigated as a model for long range DNA interactions. The ways in which PepA regulates site-specific recombination and transcription will be investigated.

data.title: The c-Jun pathway and the transcriptional control of programmed cell death in developing mammalian neurons.
data.description: I am interested in the molecular mechanisms of programmed cell death in mammalian neurons and, in particular, in how the cell death programme is regulated by signalling pathways. For these studies we have used developing nerve growth factor (NGF)-dependent sympathetic neurons, a well-characterized model of neuronal apoptosis in which cell death is transcription-dependent. When deprived of NGF, sympathetic neurons die by apoptosis and we found that the transcription factor c-Jun increases in level soon after NGF withdrawal and becomes more phosphorylated, which increases its transcriptional activity. Expression of a c-Jun dominant negative mutant protected sympathetic neurons against cell death and overexpression of wild type c-Jun could induce apoptosis in the presence of NGF indicating that c-Jun promotes cell death in sympathetic neurons. Using specific inhibitors, we subsequently showed that the increased phosphorylation of c-Jun and NGF-withdrawal induced death require Jun amino-terminal kinase (JNK) activity and that JNKs are activated by the removal of NGF. The aims of the proposed research are: 1) to further characterize the signalling pathway that leads to increased expression of c-Jun and increased c-Jun phosphorylation followed NGF withdrawal; 2) to identify c-Jun dimerization partners and transcriptional cofactors that cooperate with c-Jun to promote neuronal apoptosis; 3) to identify the step in the neuronal cell death pathway at which c-Jun functions; 4) to identify the c-Jun target genes that trigger caspase activation and apoptosis in neurons.

data.title: Molecular and cellular pathways underlying development and resolution of airway remodelling.
data.description: The aim of this project is to identify interactions between infiltrating inflammatory cells and resident lung cells that may mediate airway remodelling during allergic lung disease. This will be accomplished by examining the role of inflammatory cells, focussing on T cells, in eliciting the progression of airway remodelling in mouse models for progressive lung disease. Preliminary results indicate that the long term antigen challenge results in sustained inflammation, characterized by mononuclear rather than eosinophillic infiltration as well as bronchial smooth muscle cell proliferation, and prolonged BHR after cessation of allergen challenge. The presence of effector T cell subsets will be correlated with the development of fibrosis by using antibodies specific for Th1- or Th2-specific surface antigens. Functional roles for T cell subsets in disease progression will be determined using an atoptive transfer model, whereby antigen specific T cells are polarized in vitro and are adoptively transferred to naïve mice which are then challenged by aeorosolized antigen. Functional roles for particular mediators will be defined by in vivo blocking experiments during either allergen challenge model of the T cell transfer model. A third model will determine the effect of prior viral infection on the development of post-allergic fibrosis. Mice will be sensitized with recombinant proteins of respiratory syncytial virus before infection with the whole virus. Thereafter, mice will be assessed for evidence of fibrosis with or without additional antigen challenge. Dissection of the interactions between individual cells would be accomplished by in vitro experiments involving isolation of inflammatory leukocytes from mice after long term allergen administration and then coculture with resident lung cells (for example bronchial smooth muscle, fibroblasts and epithelial cells). Evidence of secretion of profibrotic growth factors would then be examined.

data.title: Regulation of eukaryotic microtubule nucleation and microtubule-mediated cell polarity.
data.description: I will study microtubule organization and the control of cell polarity in fission yeast. I showed that disruption of microtubules in fission yeast leads to reproducible alterations in cell morphology. This implies that normal maintenance of cell polarity requires a normal stereotyped interphase microtubule array. At present very little is known concerning how dynamic microtubules achieve a steady-state organization in eukaryotic cells. I plan to investigate this regulation at a molecular level in fission yeast, using a combination of microscopy, genetics and biochemistry. I have constructed yeast strains expressing a Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP)-tubulin fusion protein at physiological levels and have begun to characterize microtubule dynamics in vivo using time-lapse wide-field fluorescence deconvolution microscopy. These experiments indicate that fission yeast will serve as a good model eukaryote for the study of microtubule dynamics. Microtubule dynamics will be assayed in vivo by time-lapse deconvolution microscopy using existing morphological mutants as well as mutants isolate in a new screen, in order to identify genes involved in regulation of dynamics. These will be further characterized at a molecular and genetic level to determine how and where individual gene products act in the cell to modulate dynamics and interactions of microtubules with the cell cortex. In vitro assays will also be used to identify which gene products interact directly with microtubules, and their modes of action. A second aspect of my work has demonstrated that changes in fission yeast cell morphology in response to microtubule disruption are mediated through the redistribution of cortical- or plasma membrane-associated proteins that locally regulate cell polarity and sites of cell growth. These proteins are widely conserved among eukaryotes and thus understanding their mode of redistribution will help to understand how polarity is regulated in more complex situations such as cell migration in higher eukaryotic cells. As a paradigm for addressing this problem I will focus on the protein ral3p, which undergoes dynamic movements in the normal cell cycle and in response to microtubule disruption. The structure and composition of a "ral3p protein complex" will be analyzed under a number of different conditions to identify specific biochemical modifications that accompany changes in ral3p distribution. The functional significance of these changes will be determined by reverse genetics. This will be done in concert with experiments to measure fluorescence redistribution after photobleaching (FRAP) of ral3p-GFP fusion proteins at the cell cortex.
